stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Oral vaccines often produce weaker immune responses in children in some low-income regions than in children elsewhere, a gap long blamed on poor nutrition. However, immunologist Dalia Ferrante found that the gap persisted even among well-nourished children in those regions. It largely disappeared, though, among children who had recently been treated for intestinal infections. Ferrante therefore hypothesizes that ______
choices: poor nutrition prevents children from responding strongly to any kind of vaccine.
intestinal infections, rather than poor diet, weaken children's responses to oral vaccines.
children in these regions are born with immune systems that respond weakly to vaccines.
oral vaccines would outperform injected vaccines if intestinal infections were treated first.
explanation: The surprise is that good nutrition did not close the gap, but treating intestinal infections did. The one explanation that fits both details is that the infections, not diet, are what weaken the response to oral vaccines. Notice that the passage opens with the popular view (nutrition) and then undercuts it, so the blank completes the corrected view.

A.why: You went with the popular view the passage sets up to knock down. Well-nourished children still showed the gap, so nutrition can't be the explanation. The passage also never mentions 'any kind of vaccine'.

C.why: This sounds scientific but ignores a key detail: the gap largely disappeared after treatment for infection. An inborn weakness wouldn't go away because an infection was treated.

D.why: The passage never compares oral vaccines with injected ones. To get here you had to add a comparison the text never makes.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Excavations at Tell Varesh, a settlement some 300 kilometers from the nearest coast, have uncovered bones of sea bream, a fish that lives only in salt water. The remains include many vertebrae and ribs but almost no skull bones. This pattern matches the waste left by fish that are beheaded and salted before being shipped, because the heads are discarded where the fish are processed. The excavators therefore hypothesize that ______
choices: sea bream once lived in freshwater lakes located near Tell Varesh.
the sea bream were prepared for transport before reaching Tell Varesh.
residents of Tell Varesh preferred sea bream to fish from local rivers.
whole sea bream were carried to Tell Varesh and cleaned at the site.
explanation: There are two puzzles: a saltwater fish turns up far inland, and its skulls are missing. Heads are discarded where fish are processed, so processing must have happened somewhere else. The fish arrived already beheaded and salted, which explains both how they got so far inland and why the skulls are absent.

A.why: The passage says sea bream live only in salt water, so a freshwater population near the site contradicts what you were told.

C.why: The passage says nothing about local river fish or what residents preferred. You added a comparison the evidence doesn't contain.

D.why: This ignores the missing skulls. If whole fish had been cleaned at Tell Varesh, the heads would have been thrown away there and the skull bones would show up in the remains.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Polyphenols in tea bind to the form of iron found in plant foods, reducing how much of it the gut absorbs. The form of iron found in meat, however, is absorbed through a separate pathway that polyphenols do not affect. In a planned study, one group will drink tea with a lentil-based meal, and another will drink tea with a meal containing the same amount of iron that comes mainly from beef. The researchers anticipate that ______
choices: tea will reduce iron absorption about equally for the two groups.
tea will reduce iron absorption more for the beef group than the lentil group.
tea will reduce iron absorption more for the lentil group than the beef group.
the lentil group will absorb none of the iron contained in its meal.
explanation: Polyphenols block plant iron but not meat iron. The lentil meal's iron is the plant form, so tea should cut its absorption. The beef meal's iron is mostly the meat form, which tea doesn't affect. So you should predict a bigger reduction for the lentil group.

A.why: This ignores the comparison the study is built around. The passage tells you the two forms of iron respond differently to polyphenols, so the effect can't be equal.

B.why: You got the direction of the effect backwards. Polyphenols affect plant iron, not meat iron, so the lentil group is the one whose absorption tea should reduce.

D.why: The passage says polyphenols reduce absorption, not that they stop it entirely. 'None' claims more than the text supports.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Engineers in Halvorsen County expected sunlit stretches of asphalt road to wear out fastest, since heat softens asphalt and lets heavy trucks press ruts into it. Instead, stretches shaded by overpasses have needed repair nearly twice as often. Inspections show that after storms, water lingers on the shaded stretches for days, seeping into small cracks where it repeatedly freezes and expands. The engineers therefore hypothesize that ______
choices: on these roads, freezing of trapped water causes more damage than heat softening does.
heavy trucks travel the shaded stretches of these roads more often than the sunlit ones.
heat softening causes no damage at all to the asphalt roads in Halvorsen County.
the shaded stretches of these roads are softened by heat more than sunlit ones are.
explanation: The surprise is that shaded road fails more often than sunlit road. The inspections tell you what is different about the shade: water lingers there, gets into cracks, and freezes again and again. If that freeze damage outweighs the heat damage, every detail makes sense.

B.why: This explanation sounds reasonable but ignores the key detail the passage gives you, the lingering water that freezes in the cracks. Nothing in the text says anything about where trucks drive.

C.why: The passage only shows that heat is the smaller problem, not that it causes no damage. 'No damage at all' goes beyond the evidence.

D.why: Shaded stretches get less sun, so this reverses the passage's logic. The text links the shaded damage to water and freezing, not heat.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Small earthquakes beneath the Velmar Plateau, far from any boundary between tectonic plates, were long attributed to slow strain building within the crust. However, seismologist Ines Kald noticed that the quakes cluster in the months following the plateau's rainy season and nearly vanish during droughts. They also occur at shallow depths that groundwater can reach. Kald hypothesizes that ______
choices: slow strain within the crust is the sole cause of the plateau's earthquakes.
earthquakes on the plateau cause the rainy season to bring heavier rainfall.
rainwater seeping into the ground helps trigger the plateau's earthquakes.
rainfall triggers earthquakes in every region far from a plate boundary.
explanation: Two details point to water: the quakes follow the rainy season and fade in droughts, and they happen at depths groundwater can reach. The explanation that fits both is that seeping rainwater helps set them off. Note the modest wording 'helps trigger'. The passage supports a role for water, not a claim that water is the only cause.

A.why: You chose the original view that 'However' introduces in order to undercut. Calling it the 'sole' cause directly contradicts Kald's observations about rainfall.

B.why: This reverses cause and effect. The quakes follow the rainy season, so the passage points to rain influencing quakes, not quakes influencing rain.

D.why: Kald studied one plateau. Stretching her finding to 'every region' far from a plate boundary claims far more than one site can support.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Engineers inspecting a concrete highway overpass found hairline cracks along its eastern deck but none along its western deck, even though both halves were poured from the same batch of concrete on the same day. The two halves differ in one notable way: the eastern half sits directly beneath a row of sprayers that coat the road with de-icing salt each winter, while the western half receives no spray. The engineers therefore hypothesize that ______
choices: the batch of concrete used for the overpass was weaker than the engineers had originally specified.
exposure to the winter de-icing spray has contributed to the cracking along the eastern deck.
the eastern and western decks carry roughly the same volume of traffic over the course of a year.
de-icing salt is the only cause of cracking in concrete overpasses that are exposed to winter weather.
explanation: The puzzle is that two halves made from the same concrete on the same day behave differently. The passage gives only one difference between them: the eastern half gets de-icing spray and the western half doesn't. The one explanation that fits every detail is that the spray has played a part in the eastern cracking. The word "contributed" claims no more than the comparison can support.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap: it sounds technical but ignores the comparison group. Both halves came from the same batch, so a weak batch would have cracked both, and the western deck has no cracks.

C.why: This may well be true, but it doesn't explain anything. A hypothesis here has to account for why only the eastern deck cracked, and equal traffic on both decks says nothing about that difference.

D.why: You let the claim grow stronger than the evidence. One overpass can suggest that salt contributed to cracking here. It can't show that salt is the only cause of cracking in every exposed overpass. Watch for "only."

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: In most temperate regions, cities are warmer than the surrounding countryside, because pavement and buildings absorb more heat during the day than fields and forests do. Climatologists studying cities in arid regions, however, noted a key difference: the land around those cities is often bare sand and rock, which heats rapidly in sunlight, while the cities themselves contain irrigated lawns and dense shade trees. The climatologists therefore anticipated that during the daytime, desert cities would ______
choices: be warmer than the surrounding desert, much as temperate cities are warmer than their countryside.
be cooler than the surrounding desert, reversing the pattern usually seen in temperate regions.
have pavement that absorbs less heat than the pavement in cities of temperate regions does.
lose much of their irrigated lawn and shade-tree cover during the hottest months of the year.
explanation: In temperate regions, the city's surfaces absorb more heat than the land around it. In the desert the roles switch: the surrounding land is bare rock and sand that heats quickly, and the city has shade and irrigated greenery. When the setup swaps which side heats faster, the expected result flips too, so the desert city should be cooler than its surroundings during the day.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap: you kept the original effect when the setup told you it would flip. The word "however" and the swapped surfaces (bare rock outside, shade trees inside) point to the reverse of the temperate pattern.

C.why: The passage never compares the pavement of desert cities with the pavement of temperate cities. You added a detail the text doesn't contain, and it explains nothing about the city-versus-desert comparison the climatologists set up.

D.why: You picked up an incidental detail and made a claim about it. The passage describes the lawns and trees as present and says nothing about them dying back. Even if they did, that wouldn't be a prediction about how the city's temperature compares with the desert's.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Collectors have long regarded certain impressions of Dutch printmaker Aleida Voss's 1652 etching River Mill as forgeries, because the finest lines (the ripples on the water, the grain of the wooden wheel) appear faint or are missing entirely. Conservator Pieter Langeveld points out, however, that a tiny accidental scratch near the mill door appears in exactly the same place on both the crisp and the faint impressions. He also notes that copper plates lose their shallowest grooves first as they wear down with use. Langeveld therefore hypothesizes that the faint impressions ______
choices: were printed from a careful copy of Voss's plate that a later forger had engraved by hand.
were printed from Voss's original plate after it had already been used for many printings.
were made by Voss herself, who wanted the water and the wheel to look softer than before.
are now valued by collectors about as highly as the crisp impressions of River Mill are.
explanation: The shared accidental scratch shows that both sets of impressions came from the same plate. The fact that copper plates lose their shallowest grooves first explains why only the finest lines faded. Together, these details point to the original plate, printed after it had worn down. That is the corrected view, which replaces the collectors' belief that the faint impressions are forgeries.

A.why: You finished the popular view instead of the corrected one. The word "however" brings in evidence against forgery: a hand-made copy wouldn't reproduce an accidental scratch in exactly the same spot. It also leaves the detail about plate wear unexplained.

C.why: Nothing in the passage mentions Voss's intentions. This choice adds an assumption the text never gives you, and it ignores the detail about worn grooves, which explains the faint lines without any deliberate choice by the artist.

D.why: This is about market value, not about how the faint impressions came to exist. Langeveld's evidence concerns the plate and its wear. A hypothesis that explains the puzzle has to deal with that.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Traffic engineers have long assumed that when a road is closed, the vehicles that used it simply move onto nearby streets. But when the city of Marlow shut a riverside avenue that had carried about 30,000 vehicles a day, counts on the parallel streets rose by only about 9,000 vehicles a day, and bus and rail ridership along the corridor barely changed. Planner Ines Okafor hypothesizes that ______
choices: most of the avenue's former traffic was absorbed by the buses and trains serving the corridor.
many trips once made on the avenue stopped being made rather than shifting to other routes.
the parallel streets took on nearly all of the vehicles that had once used the closed avenue.
closing any major road in any city will reduce the total amount of traffic in that city.
explanation: The puzzle is the missing traffic. About 30,000 vehicles a day lost their road, yet the parallel streets gained only about 9,000, and transit ridership barely moved. The 'But' tells you the engineers' assumption is being undercut. The one explanation that fits both details is that many of those trips weren't rerouted at all and simply stopped being made.

A.why: You overlooked a key detail. The passage says bus and rail ridership 'barely changed', so transit can't have absorbed most of the traffic.

C.why: You chose the popular view the passage sets up to knock down. The parallel streets gained only about 9,000 of the 30,000 vehicles, which is nowhere near all of them.

D.why: You generalized one closure in one city to every major road everywhere, and turned a hypothesis into a certainty ('will'). Nothing in the passage supports that reach.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Mice given a course of antibiotics, which clears most bacteria from the gut, produced far fewer antibodies after swallowing a vaccine against rotavirus than untreated mice did. Yet when the same vaccine was injected into muscle instead, the antibiotic-treated mice and the untreated mice produced similar levels of antibodies. Based on these results, the research team hypothesizes that ______
choices: antibiotics directly impair the antibody-producing cells found throughout a mouse's body.
gut bacteria suppress the immune system's response to vaccines that are taken by mouth.
gut bacteria help the immune system respond to vaccines that enter through the digestive tract.
injected vaccines produce stronger antibody responses than oral vaccines do in all mammals.
explanation: One result changed and one held steady. Clearing the gut bacteria weakened the response to the swallowed vaccine but made no difference to the injected one. The explanation that fits both results is that gut bacteria help the immune system respond specifically to vaccines that arrive through the gut, so losing them matters only for the oral route.

A.why: This sounds scientific but ignores the comparison group. If antibiotics damaged antibody-producing cells throughout the body, the injected vaccine would also have produced fewer antibodies, and it didn't.

B.why: You reversed the direction of the effect. Removing the bacteria lowered the oral-vaccine response, so the bacteria were helping that response, not holding it back.

D.why: The study compares antibiotic-treated mice with untreated mice, not injection with oral delivery across all mammals. You stretched one mouse experiment into a claim about every mammal.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: At a fossil site in Wyoming, paleobotanists compared leaves preserved in two rock layers. In the older layer, about 40 percent of the leaves bear holes and chew marks left by insects; in the younger layer, only about 10 percent do. The same few tree species dominate both layers, but chemical clues in the sediment indicate that the younger layer formed during a markedly cooler interval. The researchers therefore hypothesize that ______
choices: a cooler climate reduced the number or activity of leaf-eating insects in the region.
the trees in the younger layer were species that insects could not easily digest.
leaf-eating insects grew more numerous in the region as its climate became cooler.
falling temperatures caused leaf-eating insects to vanish from the entire planet.
explanation: The surprise is the drop in insect damage from 40 percent to 10 percent. The passage rules out a change in the trees, since the same species dominate both layers, and it points to one difference: the younger layer formed when the climate was cooler. A cooler climate cutting back the leaf-eating insects explains the drop using only those details.

B.why: This ignores a key detail. The passage says the same tree species dominate both layers, so a change to less edible species can't explain the drop.

C.why: You flipped the direction of the effect. Insect damage fell in the cooler layer, which points to fewer or less active insects, not more.

D.why: One site still shows insect damage on 10 percent of leaves, so the insects didn't vanish even there. Extending that to the whole planet goes far beyond what this site can support.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Paleobotanist Ines Arroyo compared fossil leaves of an extinct oak collected from two rock layers of the same age: one from an ancient river delta and one from an upland ridge 40 kilometers away. The ridge leaves were, on average, half the size of the delta leaves, but their vein patterns and surface features were identical, so they came from the same species. Because living trees tend to grow smaller leaves when water is scarce, Arroyo hypothesizes that ______
choices: the oaks on the ridge grew under drier conditions than the oaks in the delta did.
the oaks in the delta grew under drier conditions than the oaks on the ridge did.
the oaks on the ridge belonged to a separate species suited to upland ground.
every oak species of that period grew smaller leaves at higher elevations.
explanation: The puzzle is that one species grew leaves half as large in one place as in the other. The passage tells you that small leaves go with scarce water, and the ridge leaves are the small ones. So the explanation that fits every detail is that the ridge trees had less water than the delta trees. This choice uses only the leaf comparison and the stated link between leaf size and water.

B.why: You got the direction of the gap backward. The small leaves came from the ridge, so the ridge would be the drier site. Putting the drought in the delta flips the comparison the passage sets up.

C.why: This explanation sounds scientific, but it ignores a key detail. The passage says the vein patterns and surface features were identical, so the leaves came from the same species. That detail rules out a separate upland species.

D.why: Arroyo studied one species at two sites. A claim about every oak species of the period goes far past that evidence, and the passage explains the gap with water, not with elevation.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Athletes often sit in ice baths after strength training because cold water reduces next-day muscle soreness. However, sports scientist Tomasz Wierzba notes that the inflammation cold water suppresses is also one of the signals that tells muscle to rebuild larger. To test this, his team had two groups lift weights for twelve weeks: one group took ice baths after every session, while the other cycled lightly instead. Wierzba anticipated that, compared with the cycling group, the ice-bath group would ______
choices: report less soreness after sessions but gain less muscle over the twelve weeks.
report less soreness after sessions and gain more muscle over the twelve weeks.
report more soreness after sessions and gain less muscle over the twelve weeks.
report less soreness after sessions and gain no muscle over the twelve weeks.
explanation: The passage gives you two effects of cold water that point in opposite directions. It reduces soreness, and it also suppresses a signal that helps muscle grow. So compared with the cyclists, the ice-bath group should feel less sore but build less muscle. Your answer has to describe both halves of that gap.

B.why: This is the popular view that the passage sets up and then undercuts. You assumed less soreness means better recovery and more growth. Wierzba's point is that the same suppressed inflammation should mean less growth.

C.why: The first sentence establishes that cold water reduces soreness. Saying the ice-bath group would be more sore reverses the one effect the passage treats as settled.

D.why: The passage says inflammation is one of the signals for muscle growth, not the only one. Removing part of the signal supports less growth, not no growth at all. 'No muscle' is stronger than the evidence allows.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Engineers testing a polymer roof coating expected it to wear out fastest in Arizona, where ultraviolet light is far more intense than on the cloudy Oregon coast. Instead, panels on the Oregon coast cracked about twice as fast as identical panels in Arizona. The coating absorbs water, swelling when wet and shrinking as it dries. The Oregon panels went through this cycle almost daily, while the Arizona panels were rarely wet. The engineers therefore hypothesize that ______
choices: constant swelling and shrinking did more harm to the coating than Arizona's stronger sunlight did.
the Oregon panels received more ultraviolet light than the Arizona panels received over the test.
Arizona's stronger sunlight did more harm to the coating than constant swelling and shrinking did.
repeated wetting and drying will crack any roof coating faster than intense sunlight can.
explanation: The surprise is that the site with weaker sunlight produced the faster cracking. The one detail that sets Oregon apart is the near-daily cycle of swelling and shrinking. If that cycle damages the coating more than Arizona's extra UV does, every detail in the passage makes sense, including the twofold gap.

B.why: This ignores the setting. The passage says UV is far more intense in Arizona than on the cloudy Oregon coast, so you can't explain Oregon's faster cracking with more UV.

C.why: This is the engineers' original expectation, the one the results overturned. If sunlight were the bigger threat, the Arizona panels would have cracked faster, but the Oregon panels did.

D.why: The test covered one coating, which is described as absorbing water. Extending the result to any roof coating, and saying it will always happen, claims more than one test can support.
